content: The concept of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is often measured using tools such as quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs). These metrics assign a value of 1 to each year of life lived in full health, while years lived with illness or disability are assigned values less than 1, depending on the severity of the condition. The cost-effectiveness of a medical treatment can be evaluated by calculating the cost per QALY or DALY it generates. For instance, a cancer treatment that costs $1 million and provides an average of two additional years of full health to a patient would have a cost of $500,000 per QALY. However, this calculation does not imply or assign any monetary value to a year of life itself, nor does it make assumptions about the intrinsic quality of that life. Another approach to assessing quality of life involves considering factors beyond material wealth or the standard of living. For example, individuals living in rural areas or small towns often prefer to remain in these locations, even if relocating to a city would significantly improve their standard of living. This suggests that the quality of life associated with rural living holds enough value to outweigh the potential benefits of a higher standard of living in urban areas. Similarly, individuals typically require higher compensation to accept jobs that negatively impact their quality of life. Jobs involving night shifts or extensive travel often offer higher salaries, and the difference in pay can serve as an indirect measure of the value placed on quality of life. In the context of health services research, particularly within randomized controlled trials, many studies focus on measuring HRQoL rather than adopting a broader conceptualization of quality of life. These studies often prioritize the patient’s perspective, utilizing self-completed questionnaires to gather data on HRQoL. The International Society for Quality of Life was established in response to the growing interest in this area of research and serves as a valuable resource for information on the topic. Numerous organizations and agencies worldwide have also attempted to develop methods for assessing quality of life. For further exploration, external links and related sections on this topic may provide additional insights.
